title: A noncentral geometric semisimple Lie element gives a smaller nonunipotent group over an infinite field
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], and fix an algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups below are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A torus is a group which becomes $\mathbf G_m^r$ over $\bar k$, for some integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Unipotent means admitting, for some $n\geq1$, a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] into the upper unitriangular group $\mathcal U_{n,k}\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ [def-sc-general-linear-group]: its $A$-points are upper triangular matrices with all diagonal entries $1$, for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. For a smooth group $J$, $\mathfrak j=\operatorname{Lie}(J)=T_{J/k,e}$ is the tangent space at the identity [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space], with the Lie bracket induced by group commutators [def-wf-lie-algebra]. The adjoint action $\operatorname{Ad}(g)$ is the differential at the identity of conjugation by $g$. A tangent element is semisimple if its image under the differential of a faithful closed linear representation of $J$ is diagonalizable over $\bar k$. It is noncentral if $[X,Y]\ne0$ for some $Y\in\mathfrak j$. Suppose $k$ is infinite. Let $G$ be smooth and connected, and suppose $\operatorname{Lie}(G_{\bar k})$ contains a noncentral semisimple element. Then there exists a noncentral semisimple $X\in\mathfrak g$ such that the adjoint stabilizer functor $C_G(X)(A)=\{g\in G(A):\operatorname{Ad}(g)(X\otimes1)=X\otimes1\}$ is represented by a smooth closed subgroup $C\subsetneq G$. The identity component $K=C^\circ$, with its open-subscheme structure, is a smooth connected affine closed $k$-subgroup of $G$, with $\dim K<\dim G$, and $K$ is not unipotent. Here dimension is Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. In particular the conclusions concern $C^\circ$ even when $C$ is disconnected.

source.place: Propositions 17.76–17.79, printed pp.377–378, and the semisimple-centralizer case of Proposition 17.81, p.379. Use the identity component of the centralizer (Proposition 1.34, pp.16–17); it has the same Lie algebra. Nonunipotence follows from Example 17.75, p.377, and Theorem 14.5, pp.281–282.

proof.text: Choose a closed embedding $i:G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{m,k}$ by [lem-sfb-affine-group-faithful-linear-representation]. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] its differential is injective, so identify $\mathfrak g$ with a matrix subspace. The dual-number conjugation formula gives $\operatorname{Ad}(g)Z=gZg^{-1}$ and, on differentiating, $\operatorname{ad}(Y)Z=YZ-ZY$. Choose a basis of $\mathfrak g$, of dimension $d$. The coefficients $f_1,\ldots,f_d$ in $$\det(T-\operatorname{ad}(Y))=T^d+f_1(Y)T^{d-1}+\cdots+f_d(Y)$$ are polynomial functions of the coordinates of $Y$: the entries of $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$ are linear and the determinant is its permutation sum. For the given geometric noncentral semisimple element $S\in\operatorname{Lie}(G_{\bar k})=\mathfrak g\otimes_k\bar k$, its image under some faithful closed representation of $G_{\bar k}$ is diagonalizable; the arbitrary-field faithful detection clause of [lem-sfb-algebraic-lie-additive-jordan], applied over $\bar k$ to that closed immersion and to the rational representation $i_{\bar k}$, shows that $di(S)$ is diagonalizable. Diagonalize $di(S)$. Commutation on all matrices is diagonal in the matrix-unit basis, with eigenvalues the differences of its diagonal entries. Its invariant subspace $\mathfrak g_{\bar k}$ is a sum of eigenspaces, by polynomial spectral projections. Hence $\operatorname{ad}(S)$ is diagonalizable and nonzero. Some eigenvalue is nonzero, so its characteristic polynomial is not $T^d$. Thus some $f_i$ is nonzero.

Choose such a nonzero coefficient $f_i\in k[y_1,\ldots,y_d]$. A nonzero polynomial over an infinite field cannot vanish at every rational tuple: induct on the number of variables, choose values of the first $d-1$ variables making one nonzero coefficient in the last variable nonzero, and then avoid the finitely many roots of the resulting nonzero one-variable polynomial. For zero variables a nonzero constant already has nonzero value. Consequently choose $Y\in\mathfrak g(k)$ with $f_i(Y)\ne0$. Then $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$ has a nonzero eigenvalue over $\bar k$.

If $\operatorname{char}k=0$, apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-lie-additive-jordan] to $Y$ over the perfect field $k$ and put $X=Y_s$. Functoriality for the adjoint representation says that $\operatorname{ad}(X)$ is the semisimple part of $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$; its nonzero eigenvalue from step 2 persists, so $X$ is noncentral. If $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, use [lem-sfb-restricted-rational-differentiation] and put $X=Y^{[p^N]}$ for sufficiently large $N$. It lies in $\mathfrak g(k)$ and $di(X)=di(Y)^{p^N}$, while $\operatorname{ad}(X)=\operatorname{ad}(Y)^{p^N}$. Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-lie-additive-jordan] over $\bar k$ to write $di(Y)=M_s+M_n$ with commuting diagonalizable $M_s$ and nilpotent $M_n$. Choose $p^N$ at least a nilpotence exponent of $M_n$. The binomial formula in characteristic $p$ gives $di(X)=M_s^{p^N}$, which is diagonalizable; and the nonzero eigenvalue of $\operatorname{ad}(Y)$ remains nonzero on raising it to $p^N$. Thus also in this case $X$ is rational, semisimple and noncentral. No Jordan part is assumed rational over an imperfect field.

source.place: 17.74 and 17.79, printed pp.377–378; Sections 10l and 11e for restricted powers; the imperfect-field rationality detail is supplied explicitly.

proof.text: Put $M=di(X)$ and write $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$. Let $I\subseteq A$ be generated by the entries of $gM-Mg$ of the universal matrix $g\in G(A)$. Then $C=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$ is closed, affine and of finite type; it represents the required adjoint stabilizer on every commutative $k$-algebra, by the matrix formula and tangent injectivity in [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus]. A product or inverse of matrices commuting with $M$ again commutes with $M$, so the group laws restrict, giving a closed subgroup. For $Z\in\mathfrak g$, the element $1+\epsilon\,di(Z)$ belongs to $C(k[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)$ exactly when $di(Z)M-Mdi(Z)=0$. Therefore $$\operatorname{Lie}(C)=\{Z\in\mathfrak g:[Z,X]=0\}.$$ Noncentrality makes this a proper subspace, and in particular $C\ne G$.

source.place: 17.76–17.77, printed p.377: scheme equations and dual-number calculation.

proof.text: Infinitesimal conjugation by $1+\epsilon M$ induces a derivation $D:A\to A$, since it is an algebra automorphism over the dual numbers reducing to the identity; [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] ensures that this conjugation preserves $G$. On universal matrix entries it has values $(Mg-gM)_{ab}$, and on $\det(g)^{-1}$ it is zero, since determinant is invariant under conjugation. These elements generate $A$ as an algebra, so the Leibniz rule gives $I=(D(A))$. Over $\bar k$, write $M=PZP^{-1}$ with $Z$ diagonal, with diagonal entries $\lambda_a$, and use the coordinates $x'=P^{-1}xP$. On $\bar k[x'_{ab},\det(x')^{-1}]$, $D$ is diagonal on monomials: $x'_{ab}$ has eigenvalue $\lambda_a-\lambda_b$ and $\det(x)^{-1}$ has eigenvalue zero. The defining ideal of $G_{\bar k}$ is $D$-stable, because infinitesimal conjugation preserves the subgroup. A stable subspace of this direct sum of eigenspaces is a sum of its eigenspaces: for each vector its finitely many eigencomponents are recovered by Lagrange interpolation polynomials in $D$. Thus the quotient $A\otimes_k\bar k$ also has an eigenspace decomposition for $D$. Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-derivation-zero-smooth] to this smooth affine algebra $A$ to conclude that $C=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$ is smooth over $k$.

source.place: 17.76, printed p.377, omitted semisimple-derivation modification of Lemma 13.6, printed p.256.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-finite-type-group-identity-subgroup] to the finite-type group $C$. Its identity component $K=C^\circ$ is a connected open and closed subgroup scheme. By [lem-pc-open-immersion-smooth-composition] it is smooth. The closed immersions into $C$ and then $G$ exhibit it as a closed affine finite-type subgroup: on affine coordinate rings these are successive quotients. Its tangent space at the identity is the same as that of $C$. Indeed the image of every dual-number tangent map has just the identity as its underlying point, and hence factors uniquely through the open subscheme $K$ by [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme]; this factorization is inverse to the tangent map of $K\hookrightarrow C$. Therefore $\operatorname{Lie}(K)=\operatorname{Lie}(C)$ as subspaces of $\mathfrak g$.

source.place: Proposition 1.34, printed pp.16–17; 17.81, printed p.379, read with the identity component as in 17.91, p.381.

proof.text: For $J=K,G$, smoothness and [lem-ag-smooth-lie-local-dimension] give $\dim_k\operatorname{Lie}(J)=\dim\mathcal O_{J,e}$, and [lem-ag-group-identity-local-dimension] identifies the latter with $\dim J$. Step 4 and step 6 make $\operatorname{Lie}(K)=\ker(\operatorname{ad}(X))$ a proper subspace of the finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$. Extend a basis of this kernel by a vector outside it and then to a basis of $\mathfrak g$; consequently $$\dim K=\dim_k\ker\operatorname{ad}(X)<\dim_k\mathfrak g=\dim G.$$ Both cited dimension results allow arbitrary fields; no algebraically closed or characteristic-zero specialization is being used.

source.place: Proposition 1.37, printed p.18, and Proposition 10.15, printed pp.190–191; dimension drop in 17.81, p.379.

proof.text: The alternating bracket gives $[X,X]=0$, so step 4 and step 6 put $X$ in $\operatorname{Lie}(K)$; noncentrality gives $X\ne0$. If $K$ were unipotent as in the statement, choose its closed embedding into $\mathcal U_{n,k}\subset\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$. Its tangent matrices are strictly upper triangular: substituting $1+\epsilon N$ in the defining equations sets diagonal and lower entries of $N$ to zero. Thus the image of $X$ is nilpotent. The arbitrary-field faithful detection assertion of [lem-sfb-algebraic-lie-additive-jordan], applied to $K$, forces the image of $X$ in the original faithful representation $i|_K$ to be nilpotent as well. That image is the diagonalizable matrix $M$ of step 3. A diagonalizable nilpotent matrix has every eigenvalue zero and is therefore zero. Tangent injectivity of $di$ from [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] gives $X=0$, a contradiction. Hence $K$ is not unipotent.
